title: 51 Effect of height of blood drops on novel blood biosenor for predicting anemia in goats
content:
Abstract
Small ruminants, such as goats, play a vital role in global agriculture, providing food, fiber, and other products. Consequently, ensuring their health and wellbeing is essential, particularly in addressing anemia caused by blood-feeding gastrointestinal parasites like Haemonchus contortus. The objective of this study was to observe the effect of blood drop height on the developed AI-driven biosensor for on-farm detection of anemia in goats by correlating blood Packed Cell Volume (PCV) values, blood splatter patterns, and blood drop height on splatter trends in PCV and FAMACHA scores to optimize anemia detection strategies.Data were collected from 150 observations, including blood splatter tests conducted from three heights (5 cm, 10 cm, and 15 cm) to assess the influence of height on splatter diameter. The study encompassed 75 adult male Spanish goats, with blood samples analyzed for PCV levels using centrifugation techniques. A small volume of 30 µL of blood was applied to glycerol-infused Whatman filter paper No. 1, and splatter patterns were recorded using a smartphone camera after 180 seconds. These images were correlated with PCV values obtained through standard analysis. Machine learning models were employed to improve detection accuracy of blood biosensor images for different FAMACHA scores. Four models, Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-nearest Neighbors (KNN), Backpropagation Neural Network (BPNN), and a Keras-based image classification model, were trained and tested using an image dataset of 1,054 samples. The dataset was split into training, testing, and validation sets in a 70:20:10 ratio. Initial findings indicated a detection accuracy of 76.06% after 10 epochs, which improved to 95.8% after optimizing model parameters. SVM achieved an overall F1 score of 74-100% for identifying PCV ranges from healthy to severely anemic animals, while BPNN showed an accuracy of 91-100% in anemia detection. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed no significant effect of height on blood splatter diameter, with a mean diameter of 1.02 mm across all heights. However, a moderate negative correlation (r = -0.584, p < 0.001) was observed between PCV and splatter diameter, suggesting that anemic goats with lower PCV values exhibit larger splatter diameters due to reduced blood viscosity. This study demonstrates that AI-driven biosensors can be a valuable tool for on-site, rapid anemia detection in livestock. The developed sensor’s semi-invasive technique requires minimal blood volume and provides timely results to improve animal health management. The findings also highlight the diagnostic potential of blood splatter patterns and PCV trends for anemia monitoring. While the effect of height on splatter diameter was negligible, the study emphasizes the importance of PCV and splatter characteristics in anemia detection. Future research should address these variables over longer periods and diverse environmental conditions to enhance diagnostic accuracy and practical applications in agricultural settings.
